mainEntity.name: What does a management company do for board meetings?

acceptedAnswer.text: Prepare and distribute the agenda and board package in advance, provide the management report and current financials, track action items from the last meeting, attend the meeting, and produce draft minutes afterward. The board still runs its meeting and makes every decision. What changes is that directors arrive briefed instead of hearing the numbers for the first time in the room.

mainEntity.name: What notice does an Illinois association have to give before a meeting?

acceptedAnswer.text: The Illinois Condominium Property Act sets minimum notice requirements for board and owner meetings, and an association’s own bylaws often require more. Notice generally must be posted and delivered to owners in advance, with the annual meeting and any budget or special-assessment meeting carrying their own requirements. Because bylaws vary and the statute is amended regularly, confirm your association’s specific obligations with counsel rather than relying on how it has always been done.

mainEntity.name: When can the board meet in closed session?

acceptedAnswer.text: Illinois permits a board to close part of a meeting for a limited set of subjects — litigation, violation hearings, personnel, and matters involving an individual owner’s account among them. The limits matter: closed session is for discussion of those subjects, and votes generally belong in the open portion of the meeting. Treating closed session as a general-purpose private meeting is one of the more common governance mistakes.

mainEntity.name: An owner asked to see association records. What do we have to provide?

acceptedAnswer.text: Illinois gives owners a right to inspect and copy many association records on proper written request, within a statutory response window and subject to defined exceptions such as litigation files and other owners’ personal information. The safest posture is a documented, consistent process: log the request, confirm receipt in writing, produce what the statute requires within the deadline, and involve counsel on anything genuinely within an exception. Ignoring a records request is how a routine question becomes a lawsuit.

mainEntity.name: How do we run a clean annual election?

acceptedAnswer.text: Publish the timeline, solicit candidates, distribute notice and ballots per the bylaws, and use a counting method the association can defend afterward — including the handling of proxies and, if adopted, electronic voting. Keep the ballots and the tally. Most contested elections turn not on the vote itself but on whether the association can show its process was followed.

mainEntity.name: Does the board still control decisions with a manager in place?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. The board holds the governing authority, and every contract, expenditure, and policy remains its decision. A management company implements what the board authorizes, keeps the record, and tracks the deadlines. Any firm describing it the other way around is describing something Illinois law does not permit.

blocks.html: Professional Support for Effective Board Governance
blocks.cls: font-display font-light text-3xl lg:text-4xl text-ink leading-[1.1] mb-8

blocks.html: Serving on a community association board is a significant responsibility. Board members are volunteer leaders who must navigate complex legal requirements, manage substantial budgets, and make decisions that affect their neighbors daily lives and property values. Without professional support, board service can quickly become overwhelming, leading to burnout, poor decisions, and community conflict.
blocks.cls: text-lg text-slate-600 font-light leading-relaxed mb-6

blocks.html: Stellar Property Management provides comprehensive board support services that make effective governance achievable for every board member, regardless of their experience level. From preparing detailed meeting agendas and maintaining accurate minutes to providing governance guidance and facilitating strategic planning sessions, we give your board the infrastructure it needs to lead with confidence.
blocks.cls: text-lg text-slate-600 font-light leading-relaxed mb-6

blocks.html: Our CAI-connected management team brings continuing education and practical knowledge of community association best practices, Illinois procedures, and proven governance frameworks. We serve as an operational resource for your board, coordinate with association counsel when legal advice is needed, facilitate difficult conversations, and document decisions for consistent follow-through.

blocks.html: Investing in Board Education
blocks.cls: font-display font-light text-3xl lg:text-4xl text-ink leading-[1.1] mb-8

blocks.html: The most effective association boards are the ones that invest in their own development. Board members who understand their fiduciary duties, know how to read financial statements, and are familiar with Illinois association law make better decisions, avoid costly mistakes, and create healthier communities. That is why board education is a cornerstone of our governance support services.
blocks.cls: text-lg text-slate-600 font-light leading-relaxed mb-6

blocks.html: Our new board member orientation program covers everything an incoming director needs to know: the association governing documents, current financial position, pending projects, vendor contracts, and ongoing legal matters. We also provide training on fiduciary responsibilities, open meeting requirements, and the basics of Robert Rules of Order so new members can contribute meaningfully from their very first meeting.
blocks.cls: text-lg text-slate-600 font-light leading-relaxed mb-6

blocks.html: For experienced boards, we offer annual continuing education sessions on topics like reserve fund management, insurance coverage optimization, vendor contract negotiation, and conflict resolution. We also facilitate strategic planning retreats that help boards step back from day-to-day operations and focus on the long-term vision for their community. These investments in board development pay dividends in better governance, fewer conflicts, and stronger communities.
